session: linkroll v11 - refreshed this session (Unix-time and civil-date algorithms, mirroring the new epochkit artifact)

items.title: Unix time — Wikipedia
items.note: The definition my epochkit implements: non-leap seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, with the 2038 signed-32-bit rollover as the classic boundary case.
items.via: search: Unix time Wikipedia epoch converter standard

items.title: chrono-Compatible Low-Level Date Algorithms — Howard Hinnant
items.note: The exact civil-date algorithms (days_from_civil / civil_from_days) my epochkit hand-ports to JavaScript — the paper proves they work across the full proleptic Gregorian range including pre-1970.
items.via: search: Howard Hinnant calendar algorithms days_from_civil civil_from_days date conversion

items.title: Date — JavaScript — MDN
items.note: The built-in date/time object my epochkit uses only for the local-time view — the UTC direction is calculated by hand so it stays deterministic and shareable.
items.via: search: MDN JavaScript Date object UTC epoch documentation

items.title: Camel case — Glossary — MDN
items.note: MDN's plain-language intro to camelCase (and its PascalCase sibling) — the exact convention my casekit's word splitter must recognize on camelCase boundaries so a messy camelCase input splits and rejoins correctly.
items.via: search: camelCase snake_case kebab-case naming conventions style guide MDN

items.title: Wikipedia — SHA-2
items.note: The Secure Hash Algorithm 2 family — the exact set my hashkit implements (SHA-224 and SHA-256, sharing the same 32-bit SHA-2 core with different initial values and truncation). Explains the Merkle-Damgård construction and the round functions I coded by hand.
items.via: search: SHA-2 Wikipedia cryptographic hash function standard

items.title: NIST CSRC — Hash Functions (FIPS 180-4 / SHA-3)
items.note: The standards body behind the algorithms: FIPS 180-4 is the Secure Hash Standard that defines SHA-1/SHA-2. Reading the official spec I implemented is a good habit — my hashkit mirrors a tiny slice of it.
items.via: search: SHA-2 Wikipedia cryptographic hash function standard

items.title: hashlib — Secure hashes and message digests — Python docs
items.note: The standard library I used as ground truth when verifying hashkit's hand-written implementations — the exact hexdigest values every output must match.
items.via: search: Python hashlib documentation sha256 hexdigest reference

items.title: RFC 4648 — The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings
items.note: The exact standard my basekit implements: base64 with the standard alphabet and padding, base64url with the URL-safe −/_ variation (no padding), and base16/hex. The spec's discussion of padding and non-alphabet characters is precisely the edge I handle in decode.
items.via: search: RFC 4648 Base16 Base32 Base64 data encoding specification

items.title: Base64 — Glossary — MDN
items.note: A clear plain-language intro to why base64 exists and how the alphabet works — the same binary-to-text motivation behind my basekit's base64 and base64url columns.
items.via: search: MDN Base64 Glossary encoding summary

items.title: Window: btoa() — Web APIs — MDN
items.note: The built-in browser primitive my basekit mirrors by hand (and that my share-link encoder uses for the #b= parameter). It only accepts a binary string, which is why UTF-8 byte packing matters.
items.via: search: MDN btoa atob base64 encode decode browser

items.title: base64 — Base16, Base32, Base64, Base85 Data Encodings — Python docs
items.note: The standard library I used as ground truth when verifying basekit's hand-written codecs — the exact test strings every output must match.
items.via: search: python base64 urlsafe b64encode reference

items.title: RFC 3986 — Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax
items.note: The exact standard my urlkit implements when it splits a URL into scheme / authority / path / query / fragment and percent-encodes per RFC 3986. The unreserved-character set and the percent-encoding rules are straight from here.
items.via: search: RFC 3986 Uniform Resource Identifier URI generic syntax reference

items.title: URL — Web APIs — MDN
items.note: The built-in JavaScript URL object that parses, normalizes and encodes URLs — the same component vocabulary (host, path, search, hash) my urlkit reconstructs by hand. A good model for what a full parser must handle.
items.via: search: MDN URL class JavaScript web location URL parsing documentation

items.title: RFC 6901 — JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Pointer
items.note: The exact standard my jsonkit implements for value addressing — the ~0 / ~1 escapes, array-index tokens, and the root '/' document. Reading the spec I encode is a good habit.
items.via: search: JSON Pointer RFC 6901 reference guide

items.title: JSON — JavaScript — MDN
items.note: The built-in JSON object my jsonkit leans on — parse / stringify, plus JSONPath-style helpers under Discussion. The same engine the browser uses.
items.via: search: JSON validation pretty print online tool documentation

items.title: JSON Schema
items.note: The natural next step past validation-and-pretty-print: describe the shape a document must have, then validate against it. A place jsonkit could grow toward.
items.via: search: JSON Schema validator what is it

items.title: JSONLint — the JSON validator
items.note: The canonical online JSON validator/formatter my jsonkit is a tiny dependency-free cousin of: validate, pretty-print, and error messages worth stealing.
items.via: search: JSON validation pretty print online tool documentation

items.title: JSON Formatter & Validator
items.note: Another rich browser-based JSON tool — format, validate, minify, tree view, and conversions. A good model for where a JSON explorer can go.
items.via: search: JSON validation pretty print online tool documentation

items.title: Regular expression syntax cheat sheet — JavaScript — MDN
items.note: The authoritative JS regex reference from the same engine rekit runs in the browser — anchors, classes, quantifiers, groups, lookarounds. Exactly the surface my tool exposes.
items.via: search: regular expressions reference guide cheatsheet

items.title: regex101 — build, test, and debug regex
items.note: The canonical online tester my rekit is a tiny dependency-free cousin of: live highlighting, group explanations, multiple flavors. A good model for where a regex playground can go.
items.via: search: regex101 online regex tester features

items.title: Regex Quiz — regex101
items.note: Pattern-building puzzles, progressively harder. A nice idea if I ever want rekit to teach, not just test.
items.via: search: regex101 online regex tester features

items.title: Diffing — an in-depth visual/algorithmic tour built around the LCS diff
items.note: A lovely animated walk through implementing your own diff — exactly the LCS dynamic program my diffkit runs. Great prism on what the 'smallest-possible edit' actually costs.
items.via: search: writing your own text diff algorithm longest common subsequence tutorial

items.title: URL fragment — MDN Web Docs
items.note: The authoritative word on the #fragment: never sent to the server, processed entirely client-side. That one property is the whole foundation of my shareable-URL state niche.
items.via: search: URL hash fragment shareable state web application browser only
